title: Republicans Embrace the Vice Economy
author: Brad Wilcox
content:
![Republicans Embrace the Vice
Economy](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/AP26142637098194.jpg)

As marijuana use
[_surpasses_](https://x.com/CharlesFLehman/status/2081836378950709455?ref=compactmag.com)
alcohol and tobacco use for the first time, Republicans have delivered another
win for the vice economy. Figures ranging from Donald Trump to Rand Paul
successfully pushed to delay a ban on intoxicating hemp-derived products. This
is the latest in a string of pro-vice moves from the GOP, ranging from
rescheduling marijuana by executive order to curtailing regulatory scrutiny on
cryptocurrency and prediction markets.

Given their self-conception of sturdy American virtues such as thrift, hard
work, and sobriety, you'd think the GOP would be at the forefront in opposing
Big Weed and online gambling. But too many in the party of "family values"
have become partisans for the vice economy.

> **** "Young men have been hit hardest."

Young men have been hit hardest by the proliferation of gambling apps, [
_prediction markets_](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/polymarket-
probe-ended-by-doj-in-win-for-crypto-bets-under-trump?ref=compactmag.com),
chatbot companions, [ _digital
tokens_](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/14/us/politics/sec-crypto-firms-
trump-investigation.html?ref=compactmag.com), and harmful [
_substances_](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/18/us/politics/trump-marijuana-
reclassify-order.html?ref=compactmag.com), the proliferation of which has been
helped along by the libertine wing of the Republican Party. The consequences
are clear in new [_data_](https://ifstudies.org/report-brief/americas-
demoralized-men-part-ii-lost-pathways-greater-struggles?ref=compactmag.com)
from the Institute for Family Studies, based on a survey of 2,000 men aged
18-29. Forty-three percent agree that "I am inclined to think that I am a
failure." Sixty-one percent say they often feel they have little control over
the things that happen to them. Almost half agree that they will never achieve
the American dream.

Male loneliness is rampant. In the past thirty days, a quarter of young men
report having felt lonely all or most of the time, and 26 percent felt
isolated. Forty-two percent report two or fewer close friends, including 9
percent who have zero.

Young men aren't simply lonely, sad, and pessimistic. They have noble goals of
working hard, getting married, having a family, and contributing to their
communities. But a substantial portion of young men feel like they're falling
short and making little progress towards their goals.

Rather than help them realize these dreams, too many Republicans are content
with turning them over to the very vices that will keep them emasculated;
unable to become the providers, protectors, and parents they would like to be.
More than half of young men gamble, with 35 percent doing so daily or several
times a week--a number which is even higher among conservative young men, 47
percent of whom gamble daily or several times a week. Likewise, 43 percent
watch porn daily or several times a week. An even greater number, two thirds
of young men, play video games many times a day or at least once a day.

The young men who gamble and watch pornography most regularly are more likely
to consider themselves a failure than those who do so less regularly.
Unsurprisingly, greater shares of young men who consume porn frequently say
they are lonely, anxious, and depressed than those who watch porn once a day
or less.

When it comes to gamblers, about two-thirds say that gambling creates some
level of emotional distress. Much of this emotional distress is either
"moderate" or "mild" according to the data. But these numbers will only rise
as online prediction markets and sports betting casinos continue to
proliferate.

It is unclear which comes first--the mental health problems or the gambling
and porn addictions. What is evident is that these vices are not helping young
men feel more confident in their ability to move towards their goals.

John Adams wrote that our Constitution was made for a "moral and religious
people" and was "wholly inadequate to the government of any other." The
American founders were not libertarian about vice. They understood that a
republic whose young men cannot govern themselves will not govern anyone else
for long. A political vision for American men necessitates rediscovering the
fact that liberty and license are not the same thing.

There is nothing conservative about a government that signs [ _stablecoin
bills_](https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-stablecoins-congress-
cryptocurrency-94fa3c85e32ec6fd5a55576cf46e58ea?ref=compactmag.com) while
working-class men [ _max
out_](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w33108/w33108.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
[ _credit
cards_](https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr1184.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
on parlays. There is nothing populist about a regulatory apparatus that
protects Polymarket's revenue and lets [ _insider
trading_](https://www.wsj.com/finance/regulation/government-prediction-
markets-betting-2126dcb3?ref=compactmag.com) run wild. There is nothing
Christian about canonizing THC dispensaries, sportsbooks, vapes, and AI
mistresses as the patron saints of liberty.

The political calculation for expanding the vice economy was always simple:
Republicans must do this to win young male voters. But young men are [
_increasingly souring_](https://www.economist.com/united-
states/2026/05/03/young-men-are-souring-on-donald-trump?ref=compactmag.com) on
President Trump because of [ _practical
concerns_](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/04/23/young-
voters-economy-distrust-political-system-poll/89735746007/?ref=compactmag.com)
about the cost of living and a collapse in institutional trust. As it turns
out, permission to smoke weed and gamble will not make men feel more confident
about their prospects of buying a home and one day providing for their family.

Most young men still want to get married, value financial independence, and
want to become fathers, the Institute for Family Studies [
_finds_](https://ifstudies.org/report-brief/americas-demoralized-men-
part-1?ref=compactmag.com). At the same time, they also feel deeply uncertain
about what manhood means today, and believe that society looks at manhood
negatively.

Conservatives have always understood that men flourish as devoted husbands,
fathers, workers, citizens, churchgoers, and members of their communities. But
many are no longer helping young men work to achieve their desires of marriage
and family by promoting the virtues that make healthy masculinity possible.

Instead, they are promoting business interests that seek to profit off male
misery. This isn't the way to make America great again.
